ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Ethical approval was granted by the Swedish Research Ethics Committee (approval no. 2024-04158-01) on November 04, 2024.
A total of 2500 participants were recruited as a part of a larger survey (which also contained measures of work-related constructs).
For several of the scales, the participants completed a fixed number of items randomly sampled (without replacement) from each of these scales.
Item selection was informed by a pilot study with responses from Swedish adults recruited through Prolific (N = 146), which contained more items than were included in this data collection.

Finally, the participants were given three randomly drawn items from each of five scales measuring belief in conspiracy theories regarding sham democracy (5 items, e.g., "Democratic elections in our country are being manipulated by powerful elites", partly inspired by Thomas et al., 2025), political correctness (5 items, e.g., "Scientific results that are not politically correct are being systematically hidden from the public"), reverse discrimination (5 items, e.g., "The judicial system gives preferential treatment to minorities such that they receive less harsh punishments"), great replacement theory (7 items, e.g., "The immigration of Muslims is part of a greater plan to make Muslims the majority in this nation", adapted from Jedinger et al., 2023; Obaidi et al., 2022; Strömbäck et al., 2024), and anti-west themes (5 items, e.g., "The US and western Europe secretly tries to steal the natural resources of other countries", adapted from Bogatyreva, 2024).
table.formatted: Finally, the participants were given three randomly drawn items from each of five scales measuring belief in conspiracy theories regarding sham democracy (5 items, e.g., "Democratic elections in our country are being manipulated by powerful elites", partly inspired by <ref type="bibr">Thomas et al., 2025)</ref>, political correctness (5 items, e.g., "Scientific results that are not politically correct are being systematically hidden from the public"), reverse discrimination (5 items, e.g., "The judicial system gives preferential treatment to minorities such that they receive less harsh punishments"), great replacement theory (7 items, e.g., "The immigration of Muslims is part of a greater plan to make Muslims the majority in this nation", adapted from <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Jedinger et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">Obaidi et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Strömbäck et al., 2024)</ref>, and anti-west themes (5 items, e.g., "The US and western Europe secretly tries to steal the natural resources of other countries", adapted from Bogatyreva, 2024).

table.text: A total of 3053 British adults were recruited through Prolific, as the first wave of a larger, longitudinal research project.

This was done because the UK participant pool on Prolific deviates greatly from the general population in terms of age and education (i.e., the young and highly educated are heavily overrepresented), and both these demographic characteristics are associated with susceptibility to misinformation (e.g., Bordeleau & Stockemer, 2024; Nilsson et al., 2019; Sultan et al., 2024).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

marginal.title: Marginal Significance
marginal.summary_text: You described 2 effects with terms related to 'marginally significant'.

table.text: Although the correlations between the factors dropped considerably in ESEM, the majority remained large (≥ .30) and almost all remained significant.

Slightly higher correlations were obtained for bullshit receptivity (r s = .10, p <.001) and climate change denial (r s = .08, p < .001), and marginally significant correlations were obtained for pseudoscience belief (r s = .05, p = .014) and antisemitism conspiracy (r s = -.04, p = .028) as well (for all other cases, | r s | ≤ .04, p ≥ .053; for complete results, see supplemental documents).
table.formatted: Slightly higher correlations were obtained for bullshit receptivity (r s = .10, p <.001) and climate change denial (r s = .08, p < .001), and marginally significant correlations were obtained for pseudoscience belief (r s = .05, p = .014) and antisemitism conspiracy (r s = -.04, p = .028) as well (for all other cases, | r s | ≤ .04, p ≥ .053; for complete results, see supplemental documents).

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p ≥ .053", Text = "Slightly higher correlations were obtained for bullshit receptivity (r s = .10, p <.001) and climate change denial (r s = .08, p < .001), and marginally significant correlations were obtained for pseudoscience belief (r s = .05, p = .014) and antisemitism conspiracy (r s = -.04, p = .028) as well (for all other cases, | r s | ≤ .04, p ≥ .053; for complete results, see supplemental documents)."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p ≥ .053", Sentence = "Slightly higher correlations were obtained for bullshit receptivity (r s = .10, p <.001) and climate change denial (r s = .08, p < .001), and marginally significant correlations were obtained for pseudoscience belief (r s = .05, p = .014) and antisemitism conspiracy (r s = -.04, p = .028) as well (for all other cases, | r s | ≤ .04, p ≥ .053; for complete results, see supplemental documents)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

#### Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid `setwd()` in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author's own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No `setwd()` calls were found in any of the code files.
#### Package Installation (install.packages)

live_data_statements: A total of 2500 participants were recruited as a part of a larger survey (which also contained measures of work-related constructs).
For several of the scales, the participants completed a fixed number of items randomly sampled (without replacement) from each of these scales.
Item selection was informed by a pilot study with responses from Swedish adults recruited through Prolific (N = 146), which contained more items than were included in this data collection.

Finally, the participants were given three randomly drawn items from each of five scales measuring belief in conspiracy theories regarding sham democracy (5 items, e.g., "Democratic elections in our country are being manipulated by powerful elites", partly inspired by Thomas et al., 2025), political correctness (5 items, e.g., "Scientific results that are not politically correct are being systematically hidden from the public"), reverse discrimination (5 items, e.g., "The judicial system gives preferential treatment to minorities such that they receive less harsh punishments"), great replacement theory (7 items, e.g., "The immigration of Muslims is part of a greater plan to make Muslims the majority in this nation", adapted from Jedinger et al., 2023; Obaidi et al., 2022; Strömbäck et al., 2024), and anti-west themes (5 items, e.g., "The US and western Europe secretly tries to steal the natural resources of other countries", adapted from Bogatyreva, 2024).
A total of 3053 British adults were recruited through Prolific, as the first wave of a larger, longitudinal research project.

This was done because the UK participant pool on Prolific deviates greatly from the general population in terms of age and education (i.e., the young and highly educated are heavily overrepresented), and both these demographic characteristics are associated with susceptibility to misinformation (e.g., Bordeleau & Stockemer, 2024; Nilsson et al., 2019; Sultan et al., 2024).
Participants provided informed consent before proceeding to the survey.

info.title: The Dimensionality of Misinformation Susceptibility: General Disposition or Domain-Specific Tendencies?

author.affiliation:

Department of Behaviour and Learning

text.text: This research investigated the dimensionality of misinformation susceptibility in the form of unwarranted conspiracy theories, pseudoscience, and pseudo-profound bullshit in representative samples of Swedish (N = 2283) and British (N = 3005) adults, through CFA and ESEM with target rotation.

The results yielded strong support for weak generality, i.e., substantial correlations across types of misinformation, but little to no support for strong generality, i.e., the pattern of covariances did not suggest a dominant general factor.
Splitting the common factor into separate superordinate factors representing different categories of misinformation improved fit.

The main results were generally robust across analyses, suggesting that while people may exhibit a general tendency to be susceptible to misinformation, susceptibility also varies across sub-types of misinformation.
The proliferation of misinformation in the digital sphere is a serious and growing concern (Ecker et al., 2024; West & Bergstrom, 2021).
text.formatted: The proliferation of misinformation in the digital sphere is a serious and growing concern <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Ecker et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b114">West & Bergstrom, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: It represents a significant threat to public and private health, contributing significantly to vaccine-hesitancy and vaccine-related illness and death (Caceres et al., 2022; Lee et al., 2022) and to a prioritization of ineffective or harmful alternative treatments over evidence-based medical practices (Perlis et al., 2023).
text.formatted: It represents a significant threat to public and private health, contributing significantly to vaccine-hesitancy and vaccine-related illness and death <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Caceres et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Lee et al., 2022)</ref> and to a prioritization of ineffective or harmful alternative treatments over evidence-based medical practices <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">(Perlis et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: It also poses a threat to democracy (Lewandowsky et al., 2023), playing a key role in antidemocratic movements such as the 2021 attack on Capitol Hill in the United States (McCabe et al., 2024) and in democratic backsliding and autocratic propaganda worldwide (Druckman, 2024; Dunwoody et al., 2022).
text.formatted: It also poses a threat to democracy <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Lewandowsky et al., 2023)</ref>, playing a key role in antidemocratic movements such as the 2021 attack on Capitol Hill in the United States <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(McCabe et al., 2024)</ref> and in democratic backsliding and autocratic propaganda worldwide <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Druckman, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Dunwoody et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: There is today a wealth of research programs on people's susceptibility to various kinds of misinformation (Ecker et al., 2022; Murphy et al., 2023), including fabricated news stories ("fake news"; Lazer et al., 2018; Pennycook & Rand, 2021), conspiracy theories (Douglas & Sutton, 2023), pseudoscience (Fasce & Picó, 2019; Torres et al., 2023), and pseudo-profound nonsense or "bullshit" (Nilsson et al., 2024; Pennycook et al., 2014).
text.formatted: There is today a wealth of research programs on people's susceptibility to various kinds of misinformation <ref type="bibr">(Ecker et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Murphy et al., 2023)</ref>, including fabricated news stories ("fake news"; <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Lazer et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">Pennycook & Rand, 2021)</ref>, conspiracy theories <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Douglas & Sutton, 2023)</ref>, pseudoscience <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Fasce & Picó, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b106">Torres et al., 2023)</ref>, and pseudo-profound nonsense or "bullshit" <ref type="bibr">(Nilsson et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Pennycook et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Although multiple categories of misinformation are addressed in some research programs (e.g., Aspernäs et al., 2023; Bowes & Tasimi, 2022), there is a surprising lack of research studying the dimensionality across qualitatively different categories of misinformation-that is, the degree to which different kinds of misinformation susceptibility can be captured by a single general factor or a few superordinate factors.
text.formatted: Although multiple categories of misinformation are addressed in some research programs (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Aspernäs et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Bowes & Tasimi, 2022)</ref>, there is a surprising lack of research studying the dimensionality across qualitatively different categories of misinformation-that is, the degree to which different kinds of misinformation susceptibility can be captured by a single general factor or a few superordinate factors.

text.text: This is a substantial limitation, leading to unnecessary theoretical fragmentation.
It may also contribute to the proliferation or maintenance of jinglejangle fallacies-a pervasive problem in psychological science (Gonzalez et al., 2021).
text.formatted: It may also contribute to the proliferation or maintenance of jinglejangle fallacies-a pervasive problem in psychological science <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Gonzalez et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: A better understanding of how misinformation susceptibility is structured would help us to understand, for example, which causal explanations may be common across categories of misinformation and which interventions may be expected to generalize.

The present study therefore aimed to provide a thorough investigation of the dimensionality and covariance structure of a large battery of scales measuring receptivity to diverse forms of misinformation.
Misinformation is information that is in some sense malicious or misleading (Adams et al., 2023; van der Linden et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Misinformation is information that is in some sense malicious or misleading <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Adams et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b107">van der Linden et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This includes, for instance, information that clearly contradicts or misrepresents scientific evidence (i.e., anti-science) or that masquerades as science (i.e., pseudo-science).

Drawing on philosophical discussions about how to adjudicate between what is to be regarded as science as opposed to pseudoscience (i.e., the classical demarcation problem), this kind of misinformation can be said to lack epistemic warrant (Hansson, 2009).
text.formatted: Drawing on philosophical discussions about how to adjudicate between what is to be regarded as science as opposed to pseudoscience (i.e., the classical demarcation problem), this kind of misinformation can be said to lack epistemic warrant <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Hansson, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: This means that it has a low probability of being true, given the totality of evidence available to humans (collectively) at the time of inquiry, weighted by the epistemic division of labour in society (i.e., weighing judgments made by subject-matter experts higher).

This epistemic criterion can also be applied to beliefs that are less explicitly related to domains of science, such as conspiracy theories, which explain social and political events in terms of secret plots by powerful groups with malevolent agendas (Douglas & Sutton, 2023).
text.formatted: This epistemic criterion can also be applied to beliefs that are less explicitly related to domains of science, such as conspiracy theories, which explain social and political events in terms of secret plots by powerful groups with malevolent agendas <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Douglas & Sutton, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: For instance, Keeley (2019) refers to unwarranted conspiracy theories, which are those conspiracy theories that, regardless of the ultimate truth of the matter, are unwarranted given the epistemic situation we find ourselves in at the time-in other words, those that have the potential to misinform people.
text.formatted: For instance, <ref type="bibr">Keeley (2019)</ref> refers to unwarranted conspiracy theories, which are those conspiracy theories that, regardless of the ultimate truth of the matter, are unwarranted given the epistemic situation we find ourselves in at the time-in other words, those that have the potential to misinform people.

text.text: Analogously, recent studies (e.g., Frenken et al., 2024; Hattersley et al., 2022) have empirically distinguished belief in implausible conspiracy theories (e.g., faking the moon landing) from belief in plausible ones (e.g., nerve agent poisoning orchestrated by the Russian secret service), which do not constitute misinformation.
text.formatted: Analogously, recent studies (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Frenken et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Hattersley et al., 2022)</ref> have empirically distinguished belief in implausible conspiracy theories (e.g., faking the moon landing) from belief in plausible ones (e.g., nerve agent poisoning orchestrated by the Russian secret service), which do not constitute misinformation.

text.text: Another type of misinformation is "bullshit" which, on Frankfurt's (2005) influential analysis refers to statements or utterances designed to, for example, impress or persuade others, with no regard for their veracity.
text.formatted: Another type of misinformation is "bullshit" which, on <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Frankfurt's (2005)</ref> influential analysis refers to statements or utterances designed to, for example, impress or persuade others, with no regard for their veracity.

text.text: These do not necessarily lack epistemic warrant in every single case-a person who is bullshitting might accidentally make a warranted statement even though that was not the intention.

In cases such as this, the commonality with other forms of misinformation may lie not in the content per se but rather in the absence of epistemic conscientiousness (i.e., concern for the truth) on the part of the source spreading it (Moberger, 2020).
text.formatted: In cases such as this, the commonality with other forms of misinformation may lie not in the content per se but rather in the absence of epistemic conscientiousness (i.e., concern for the truth) on the part of the source spreading it <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Moberger, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, the specific category of pseudo-profound bullshit (Pennycook et al., 2015) is defined more in terms of intrinsic semantic properties than in terms of intentions of the agent making the utterances.
text.formatted: At the same time, the specific category of pseudo-profound bullshit <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">(Pennycook et al., 2015)</ref> is defined more in terms of intrinsic semantic properties than in terms of intentions of the agent making the utterances.

text.text: It is charactered as vacuous, obscure, pseudo-intellectual nonsense-or as "unclarifiable unclarity" in Cohen's (2002, p. 333) words (see also Buekens & Boudry, 2015; Moberger, 2020).
text.formatted: It is charactered as vacuous, obscure, pseudo-intellectual nonsense-or as "unclarifiable unclarity" in <ref type="bibr">Cohen's (2002, p. 333)</ref> words (see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Buekens & Boudry, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Moberger, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This type of bullshit necessarily lacks epistemic warrant, as it has no propositional content that could possibly be true.
In this sense, a lack of epistemic warrant is a common ingredient across all categories of misinformation under consideration.

Susceptibility to misinformation has more frequently been studied in adjacent fields, such as social, cognitive, and political psychology, than in personality psychology-and this may be one reason that its taxonomic structure has remained underexplored.
Nevertheless, this research topic is theoretically compatible with contemporary conceptualizations of personality.

It is compatible with trait theory, particularly insofar as misinformation susceptibility can be conceptualized in terms of a general disposition affecting how people interact with the world, although it is poorly accounted for by traditional lexical models, in terms of very modest correlations between 'Big Few' traits and unsubstantiated beliefs (e.g., Bowes et al., 2023; Fasce & Picó, 2019; Stasielowicz, 2022).

text.text: It is also well aligned with theoretical perspectives that emphasize the role of beliefs in personality structure (e.g., Dweck, 2017; McAdams & Pals, 2006; Nilsson, 2014).

text.text: If similar biases and thinking styles undergird, for instance, conspiratorial thinking and non-conspiratorial pseudoscientific beliefs, one would expect these to be highly correlated.

In this vein, Boudry et al. (2015) highlighted multiple mechanisms relevant to the proliferation and popular belief in pseudoscience, including evolved cognitive biases such as an (over)reliance on intuition, the intentional stance (i.e., ascribing agency, goals, desires, etc.), and a promiscuous teleology (i.e., ascribing purposefulness), while pointing out that conspiracy thinking often relies on similar biases. Douglas et al. (2016) found that people who were more likely to attribute intentionality to inanimate entities were indeed more likely to endorse conspiracy theories (for a review, see van Prooijen & Vugt, 2018).

(2016)</ref> found that people who were more likely to attribute intentionality to inanimate entities were indeed more likely to endorse conspiracy theories (for a review, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">van Prooijen & Vugt, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, an evolved human proclivity to search for meaningful patterns may help to explain belief in a wide range of unwarranted claims, including conspiracy theories, pseudoscience, pseudoprofound bullshit, and superstition (Shermer, 2011; van Prooijen & Vugt, 2018).

text.text: Studies have indeed found that the tendency to see illusory patterns in random noise is associated with susceptibility to both conspiracy theories and pseudo-profound bullshit (van Prooijen et al., 2018; Walker et al., 2019).

text.text: Furthermore, Boudry and Braeckman (2011, 2012) mention both conspiratorial thinking and obscurantism as part of an epistemic defence mechanism and potential immunising strategy for unwarranted beliefs (see also Friesen et al., 2015)-while obscurantism renders ideas vague to make them seem profound or unassailable, conspiracy theories allow the believer to dismiss criticism as an attempt to conceal the truth.

text.text: This mirrors Popper's (1959) classical analysis of pseudoscientific ideas as being immune to critique and falsification.

text.text: Another similarity is that cognitive dispositions for reflective, rational, and actively open-minded thinking tend to similarly reduce susceptibility to a wide range of misinformation, including conspiracy theories, pseudoscience, and pseudo-profound bullshit (e.g., Aspernäs et al., 2023; Pennycook et al., 2015; Torres et al., 2023).

text.text: Furthermore, studies that have taken the plausibility of conspiracy theories into account (e.g., Frenken et al., 2024; Hattersley et al., 2022) have found that associations with unreflective, biased, and intuitive reasoning are driven by the implausibility of the content rather than the conspiratorial elements per se.

text.text: Insofar as the scales capture a general tendency to believe in implausible ideas, we should expect them to correlate strongly with measures of susceptibility to other kinds of misinformation.

These similarities notwithstanding, there may also be differences in the extent to which trust in the establishment, scientific knowledge, partisanship, and other causal factors matter for susceptibility across different kinds of misinformation.

For instance, Van Prooijen and Vugt (2018) proposed an evolved mechanism for detecting hostile coalitions, which may be specific for belief in conspiracy theories-as opposed to, for instance, pseudoscience and bullshit.
This would suggest that susceptibility to different kinds of misinformation is not reducible to a single general disposition.
The dimensionality of misinformation susceptibility has been studied most extensively in the domain of conspiracy theories.
In a classical study, Goertzel (1994) found that beliefs in specific conspiracy theories-even those of little to no direct relation to each other-were often substantially correlated.

text.text: Subsequently, measures of generic conspiracist mentality or worldview were developed (Brotherton et al., 2013; Bruder et al., 2013).

text.text: Some researchers have argued that conspiracy mentality and endorsement of specific theories ought to be treated as distinct phenomena (e.g., Imhoff, 2024; Nera, 2024) and have highlighted that generic conspiracy mentality is less laden with political content (Imhoff et al., 2022; Sutton et al., 2024), although measures of conspiracist mentality and specific conspiracy theory belief tend to be highly correlated (Strömbäck et al., 2024).

(2024) found that measures of receptivity to pseudo-profound bullshit in the new age, corporate, postmodern, and ideological domains did capture some unique variation, while also sharing a substantial general factor and exhibiting similar correlations with epistemic orientations such as illusory pattern perception, subjectivism, black-and-white thinking, and lack of analytical and actively open-minded thinking.

text.text: Subsequent research has found an overlap across domains of unsubstantiated beliefs beyond, for example, just conspiracy theories vis-à-vis other conspiracy theories, suggesting a degree of generality for unsubstantiated beliefs writ large (i.e., a "generality hypothesis": Bensley et al., 2020).

text.text: This includes strong correlations between unwarranted conspiracy beliefs, pseudoscientific beliefs, receptivity to pseudo-profound bullshit, and paranormal beliefs (e.g., Aspernäs et al., 2023; Bensley et al., 2020 Bensley et al., , 2022;; Lobato et al., 2014; Ståhl & Van Prooijien, 2018).
text.formatted: This includes strong correlations between unwarranted conspiracy beliefs, pseudoscientific beliefs, receptivity to pseudo-profound bullshit, and paranormal beliefs (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Aspernäs et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Bensley et al., 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Bensley et al., , 2022;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Lobato et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Ståhl & Van Prooijien, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, Smallpage et al. (2023) found support for a second-order factor explaining the covariance between paranormal thinking, conspiracism, and pseudoscience endorsement, suggesting a high degree of interrelatedness between the three domains.

In other words, there are two related strands of previous investigations into the generality and dimensionality of unsubstantiated claims: one investigating the presence of a positive manifold where systematically substantial and significant positive correlations represent generality (e.g., Bensley et al., 2020), and a second investigating the feasibility of a shared, common factor as accounting for systematic covariance in the data (e.g., Smallpage et al., 2023), henceforth referred to as weak and strong generality, respectively.

text.text: This research comprehensively investigated the dimensionality of susceptibility to misinformation among Swedish (Study 1, N = 2283) and British (Study 2, N = 3005) adults, using a large battery of traditional and novel measures covering a diverse set of unwarranted conspiracy theories, unsubstantiated beliefs, other misinformed claims, and pseudo-profound bullshit.

To further ensure the diversity of the measures, we included both ideologically neutral types of misinformation, and misinformation aligned with left-and right-wing ideology respectively, within each category.

Additionally, we included measures of belief in some extreme types of misinformation, including conspiracy theories about electoral manipulation, Jewish elites, and a "Great Replacement" of the European population.
Four main hypotheses were tested.

The first posited a weak generality while the second, and to some extent the third and fourth, posited a strong generality: Hypothesis 1: There are substantial and significant positive correlations between different kinds of misinformed beliefs.
Hypothesis 2: A common factor of misinformation susceptibility captures the systematic, shared variance among all the measures.

Hypothesis 3: Splitting the second-order factor up into two correlated second-order factors that represent explicitly conspiratorial content and non-conspiratorial content, respectively, better accounts for the variance shared among the measures.

Hypothesis 4: Splitting the second-order factor up into three correlated second-order factors that represent left-wing, ideologically neutral, and right-wing content, respectively, better accounts for the variance shared among the measures.
The second and third hypotheses were pre-registered but reworded for clarity.
To test the hypotheses, we fitted a series of measurement models (correlated factors, second-order factors, and bifactor models) with Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA).

We thereafter used Exploratory Structural Equation Modelling (ESEM) with target rotation to investigate whether the factor correlations of the correlated factors models were inflated by unmodelled cross-loadings.

Furthermore, we calculated Explained Common Variance (ECV), which represents the proportion of common variance in the latent factor space attributable to a general factor, and the composite reliability index of the general factor (ω h ).

In Study 2, which was a replication and extension in a separate population, we also investigated whether method covariance stemming from response biases might inflate factor correlations using a marker variable technique.
This study provided an initial test of the hypotheses in a nationally representative sample of Swedish adults.

For several of the scales, we used planned missingness, to minimize the response burden (e.g., Enders, 2022; Graham et al., 2006; Rhemtulla & Hancock, 2016), while retaining a sufficient set of items to cover diverse forms of misinformation.

text.text: A sample that was representative of the Swedish adult population in terms of age, sex, and geographic location was recruited from a larger nationally representative panel by an independent research firm.
Participants received a standard monetary compensation for completing a survey administered through Qualtrics.
A total of 2500 participants were recruited as a part of a larger survey (which also contained measures of work-related constructs).

Sample size was considered sufficiently large for the intended purposes, while being within budgetary constraints of the larger research project. 217 participants who had either failed an attention check or completed the survey in less than a fourth of the median response time were excluded from analyses, leaving N = 2283 (M age = 42.4; SD age = 12.1; 47% men, 52% women; 59% with some form of post-secondary education and 38% with a high school degree or equivalent).
For several of the scales, the participants completed a fixed number of items randomly sampled (without replacement) from each of these scales.
This type of design has been shown to perform on par with other common forms of planned missing data designs, at least with large samples (Zhang & Yu, 2022).
text.formatted: This type of design has been shown to perform on par with other common forms of planned missing data designs, at least with large samples <ref type="bibr">(Zhang & Yu, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The planned missingness is Missing Completely at Random (MCAR), meaning that it does not introduce any bias in the data, and statistical techniques for handling missing data, such as Full Information Maximum Likelihood (FIML) estimation, can be leveraged to achieve statistical power close to what you would get with an equally sized sample of complete data (Enders, 2022).

text.text: Item selection was informed by a pilot study with responses from Swedish adults recruited through Prolific (N = 146), which contained more items than were included in this data collection.
The participants responded to all items except for the bullshit items on 7-point Likert scales ranging from 1 ("Definitely false") to 7 ("Definitely true").

General conspiracy mentality was measured with four items (e.g., "Most people do not realize how much our lives are governed by plans concocted in secret"), taken from Nilsson and Bäckström (2024) and originally adapted from Bruder et al. (2013).

text.text: We conducted three separate CFAs, each corresponding to a different view of underlying data generating mechanisms.
For all three models, there were 16 factors (one per scale, as delineated above) spread across 70 indicators.
Model A was a correlated factors model, where all 16 factors were allowed to covary freely with each other.
Model B was a second-order factor model with one second-order factor having loadings on all 16 first-order factors.

Model C was a bifactor model with one general factor loading on all 70 indicators directly, as well as 16 specific factors loading on the same indicators as in Models A and B (for fuller treatment of difference between these models, see Reise et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Model C was a bifactor model with one general factor loading on all 70 indicators directly, as well as 16 specific factors loading on the same indicators as in Models A and B (for fuller treatment of difference between these models, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b95">Reise et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: In Model C, the 16 specific factors were specified to be orthogonal to each other as well as to the general factor, as is standard for facilitating interpretation and preventing estimation and convergence difficulties in bifactor models.

Additionally, to test Hypothesis 3, we fitted a second-order model with two correlated second-order factors: one with loadings on the factors with explicit conspiratorial content, and one with loadings on the others.

For Hypothesis 4, we fitted a similar model with three correlated second-order factors: left-wing (financial, anti-west, terrorist attack conspiracies), neutral (pseudoscience, astrology, pseudo-profound bullshit, alien conspiracies, general conspiracism, antisemitic conspiracies), and right-wing (political correctness, great replacement, reverse discrimination, global warming denial) content.
As a robustness check, we also fitted an ESEM-model with target rotation, with primary loadings mimicking the specified factor structure of the independent-clusters CFA (ICM-CFA).

The purpose of this was to investigate whether the presence of small, positive cross-loadings fixed to zero might have led to inflated latent correlations-a problem that is likely to occur even for models with otherwise acceptable model fit (e.g., Asparouhov & Muthén, 2009; Mai et al., 2018; Marsh et al., 2010 Marsh et al., , 2013 Marsh et al., , 2014)).

Furthermore, the results provide partial support for the strong generality hypothesis, which posits that a general factor adequately accounts for individual differences in misinformation susceptibility.
On the one hand, the two models containing a general factor yielded decent indices of absolute fit (RMSEA).

The bifactor model in particular showed adequate fit based on CFI, even though the fitting propensity of bifactor models is inversely correlated with the number of specific factors (Bonifay et al., 2025).

Finally, the ECV of the general factor was .61, which means that while the general factor accounted for over half of the common variance among the latent factors, it was clearly short of what would be expected of a dominant general factor (e.g., ECV > .7-.8).

text.text: As to whether common sources of variance for non-conspiratorial vis-à-vis conspiratorial content are best modeled as separate or as one factor, we found that the fit of a model with two correlated second-order factors improved little in absolute terms, compared to its nested equivalent containing only one second-order factor.

The small change in model fit could be explained by a latent correlation between the two second-order factors of r = .89. Shi et al. (2018, p. 679) proposed that "the misfit corresponding to ρ = 0.90 [between factors with independent clusters] is substantively ignorable" in the sense of being large enough that opting for a one-factor model makes sense for the purpose of parsimony.

(2018, p. 679)</ref> proposed that "the misfit corresponding to ρ = 0.90 [between factors with independent clusters] is substantively ignorable" in the sense of being large enough that opting for a one-factor model makes sense for the purpose of parsimony.

text.text: Accordingly, these results could be interpreted as failing to support a meaningful, statistical distinction between conspiratorial and non-conspiratorial misinformation susceptibility.

Nevertheless, the sheer size of the model still means that there are large amounts of unmodeled cross-loadings that likely greatly inflated the latent correlation between the two higher-order factors.
This should invite caution in interpreting these results too strongly.

By contrast, dividing up the first-order factors between three second-order factors representing hypothesized ideological alignment of item content (right-wing, left-wing, neutral) resulted in significant and marked improvements in model fit relative to the other two second-order models, particularly in terms of the incremental fit indices.
This suggests that the ideological tilt of the misinformation could account for systematic (co)variances in the data better than the rival models.
Another result worth noting is that initial analyses suggested that the factors representing misinformed beliefs about the effects of genes (blank slateism) and IQ yielded poor model fit.
In other words, endorsement of these beliefs seemed to represent something relatively unique compared to the other measures included.
Finally, the CFA-based factor correlations between general conspiracy mentality and specific conspiracy theories were generally at least as large as those between the specific conspiracy theories.

Furthermore, these correlations dropped considerably relative to the other factors in the ESEM and the factor loading matrix showed relatively small primary loadings and relatively large secondary loadings for the conspiracy mentality factor, suggesting that there was difficulty differentiating this factor from the others.
In other words, it may function more as a general factor than as a unique, correlated factor alongside the others.

This pattern is consistent with previous literature describing conspiracy mentality as a generalized disposition, worldview, or political attitude (Imhoff & Bruder, 2014; Nera, 2024), reflecting core ingredients of conspiratorial thinking, such as anti-authority or anti-establishment stances (Imhoff, 2024).

This study replicated and extended the first study in a British quota sample.
The survey included the same scales as in the first study, except that two items measuring belief in paranormal phenomena (categorized as ideologically neutral misinformation) were added.
We shortened a few of the scales to reduce the response burden on participants without requiring planned missingness.

Furthermore, the survey contained a subset of items unrelated to the study's focal constructs (i.e., a "marker variable", Williams et al., 2010), which allowed us to test the degree to which the measures were contaminated by method variance (Maydeu-Olivares & Steenkamp, 2025) producing spuriously high correlations.

text.text: Insofar as the marker variable and the constructs of interests are theoretically unrelated, any correlation between them should reflect only common method variance.
A total of 3053 British adults were recruited through Prolific, as the first wave of a larger, longitudinal research project.
Sample size was determined by availability of resources and power calculations for future longitudinal analyses, with expected rates of attrition taken into account.

The sample was stratified to contain an equal number of individual with/without higher education and the proportions of individuals in three age categories (18-34, 35-49, 50+) were calibrated against UK census data within both education strata.

This was done because the UK participant pool on Prolific deviates greatly from the general population in terms of age and education (i.e., the young and highly educated are heavily overrepresented), and both these demographic characteristics are associated with susceptibility to misinformation (e.g., Bordeleau & Stockemer, 2024; Nilsson et al., 2019; Sultan et al., 2024).

text.text: The participants completed a Qualtrics-survey.

Those who failed more than one out of three attention checks, completed the survey in less than a fourth of the median sample response time, or only completed initial parts of the survey were excluded, leaving 3005 participants (M age = 43.3; SD age = 13.6; 55% women, 43% men; 76% with some form of post-secondary education and 23% with an upper secondary school degree or equivalent as highest level of education).
The participants responded to all items except for the bullshit items on 7-point Likert scales ranging from 1 ("Definitely false") to 7 ("Definitely true").
Several scales were shortened, and in a handful of cases, items were substituted (for full list of measures, see supplemental documents).

However, all models failed to converge when treating general conspiracy mentality and belief in conspiracy theories about sham democracy as separate factors-and the latent correlation between these factors was as high as .99 when we manually inspected the Φ-matrix of a correlated factors model that failed to converge.
Consequently, the two scales were collapsed into a general conspiracism factor in all models, which consistently resolved the estimation issues.
The model with two correlated second-order factors still resulted in non-convergence and a Heywood-case, however.
Inspection of the ϴ-matrix revealed that the first indicator for the climate change denial factor had a negative residual (with a standardised factor loading of λ = .97).
We constrained the residual variance of this item to the same small yet positive, estimated value in the model with only one second-order factor, which converged successfully.

To be able to compare this model to the other second-order factor models (i.e., to make the models nested), we applied the same constraint to the residual of the same item for all the second-order models involved in testing Hypotheses 2, 3, and 4.
Furthermore, there were some issues related to the information matrix of the fully orthogonally specified bifactor model (for more details, see supplementary materials).

Rather than report (misleadingly good) fit indices for a bifactor model where specific factors are allowed to covary, we chose to focus on the second-order model as representing a common factor model in this study.
We did use the factor loading matrix and residual (co)variance matrix of a successfully converged orthogonal bifactor model solely for the purpose of calculating ECV and ω h for this study as well.

To investigate common method covariance across scales, we ran zero-order bivariate correlations between the index scores of the marker variable and the substantive constructs of interest, reporting Spearman's rho due to the skewness (-.099) of the marker variable.
As some factors had only two indicators in this study, Principal Axis Factoring instead of CFA was used for deriving the Omega-total coefficient for these factors.

text.text: However, model fit was still subpar in the absolute sense (in terms of incremental fit indices), as could be expected based on the latent correlations.

Correlations between the marker variable and index scores for the substantive factors were close to zero and non-significant in most cases, despite the large sample size (average absolute correlation across all factors: r s = .03).

Slightly higher correlations were obtained for bullshit receptivity (r s = .10, p <.001) and climate change denial (r s = .08, p < .001), and marginally significant correlations were obtained for pseudoscience belief (r s = .05, p = .014) and antisemitism conspiracy (r s = -.04, p = .028) as well (for all other cases, | r s | ≤ .04, p ≥ .053; for complete results, see supplemental documents).
text.formatted: Slightly higher correlations were obtained for bullshit receptivity (r s = .10, p <.001) and climate change denial (r s = .08, p < .001), and marginally significant correlations were obtained for pseudoscience belief (r s = .05, p = .014) and antisemitism conspiracy (r s = -.04, p = .028) as well (for all other cases, | r s | ≤ .04, p ≥ .053; for complete results, see supplemental documents).

text.text: These results suggest that the amount of systematic method covariance related to response biases in the data was negligible overall relative to the strong covariances between the substantive factors of interest.
The results were once again mostly supportive of the weak generality hypothesis, with substantial correlations between most primary factors.

There was, however, greater variation in the magnitude of the latent correlations in this study (e.g., around a fourth of them were weak), and the strong generality hypothesis was not supported at all, as the ECV indicated that the general factor accounted for less than half of the common variance among latent factors, which is substantially below what could reasonably be expected given a dominant general factor.

Furthermore, this study yielded clear evidence for a meaningful distinction between conspiratorial and non-conspiratorial forms of misinformation susceptibility, with significant improvements in model fit when these were split up into separate second-order factors rather than lumped together.

Interestingly, the improvement in model fit was even larger when left-wing, ideologically neutral, and right-wing forms of misinformation were represented by separate second-order factors, suggesting that ideological tilt plays a key role in what kinds of misinformation people endorse.
There were generally stronger correlations between the conspiratorial factors than between those without conspiratorial content, suggesting more of a common core for these, as might be expected.

In fact, conspiracy mentality overlapped with conspiracy theories regarding sham democracy to such a degree that we had to collapse the two factors into a general conspiracist ideation factor for the models to converge.
This was plausibly because both scales contained items expressing conspiracist narratives about the political system.

Furthermore, the latent correlations between this factor and belief in other more specific conspiracy theories were consistently very strong, consistent with the notion that it captured general ingredients of conspiratorial thinking, such as anti-authority or anti-establishment stances (Imhoff, 2024).
text.formatted: Furthermore, the latent correlations between this factor and belief in other more specific conspiracy theories were consistently very strong, consistent with the notion that it captured general ingredients of conspiratorial thinking, such as anti-authority or anti-establishment stances <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Imhoff, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: There was one notable exception, where an equally strong correlation emerged between conspiratorial and non-conspiratorial contents: belief in conspiracies about a coverup of extraterrestrial activity had a very strong latent correlation with paranormal beliefs-stronger than with any of its conspiratorial siblings, in fact-and strong correlations also with belief in astrology and pseudoscience.
These results point to a possible common core of mystical, magical, or new age thinking influencing misinformation susceptibility irrespective of conspiratorial content.

At the same time, belief in pseudoscience loaded much higher on the aggregated second-order factor than other non-conspiratorial factors did-and in fact higher than most of the conspiratorial ones as well-suggesting that this particular scale captured misinformation susceptibility more broadly, beyond new age thinking.

Another noteworthy finding is that there were stronger and more consistent correlations between factors representing susceptibility to misinformation with a right-wing ideological tilt (i.e., global warming denial and conspiracy theories about liberal elites) than among those with a left-wing tilt.
In fact, IQ-denial and blank slateism, which were assumed to represent left-wing misinformation, exhibited the most uniqueness out of all the scales.
The inclusion of marker variables allowed us to assess the potential influence of response style biases inflating correlations.

Pseudo-profound bullshit receptivity stood out in terms of having a slightly higher correlation with the marker variable compared to other factors, suggesting that there may have been a small degree of response style bias affecting this measure more than the others.
A possible reason could be that the measurement places a higher cognitive demand on participants, resulting in participants defaulting to a response style more agnostic of item content.

At the same time, the correlations between the substantive factors and the marker variable were negligible overall, particularly compared to the very strong covariation between the substantive factors, suggesting that systematic method variance had little effect on the factor structure.

The discrepancies in the strength of results across the two studies may have been, at least partly, the result of poorer data quality in Study 1, with more careless responding and response styles biases inflating the latent correlations.

While we did not formally test whether the latent correlations were indeed more inflated by systematic method covariance in Study 1, we see no clear theoretical reason that various forms of misinformation susceptibility should be substantially less differentiated in a Swedish population than in a British one.
In Study 2, not only were the overall correlations among measures in the data lower, but they were also more systematically in line with theoretical expectations.

For instance, in Study 1, pseudoprofound bullshit receptivity showed latent correlations with other factors roughly comparable to those of the other variables, while in Study 2, it had substantially lower correlations with the other aspects of misinformation receptivity.

The Study 2 result is more in line with expectations provided both that pseudo-profound bullshit receptivity constitutes a qualitatively different kind of misinformation (i.e., nonsense without propositional content), measured with different response anchors and a different set of instructions (i.e., about rating the profundity of a statement rather than its truth).
Based on this alone, one would expect careful and conscientious respondents to differ more in their inclinations to score a certain way on bullshit, as was the case in study 2.

Despite an increased interest in the psychology of misinformation susceptibility, researchers have paid little attention to whether it reflects a general tendency that cuts across domains or a set of largely distinct, domain-specific tendencies.
As a result, potential commonalities across categories of misinformation have been underexplored, leaving the literature fragmented and disorganized.

Although several studies have shown correlations across different kinds of misinformation (Aspernäs et al., 2023; Bensley et al., 2020 Bensley et al., , 2022;; Lobato et al., 2014; van Prooijen et al., 2018), the dimensionality across measures had not previously been rigorously examined.
text.formatted: Although several studies have shown correlations across different kinds of misinformation <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Aspernäs et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Bensley et al., 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Bensley et al., , 2022;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Lobato et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">van Prooijen et al., 2018)</ref>, the dimensionality across measures had not previously been rigorously examined.

text.text: In the current research, we therefore investigated the covariance structure of misinformation susceptibility using a large battery of measures covering belief in unwarranted conspiracy theories, antiscientific and pseudoscientific statements, and pseudo-profound bullshit in two large samples of Swedish and British adults.

The findings generally provide evidence for weak generality (Bensley et al., 2020 (Bensley et al., , 2022;; Lobato et al., 2014), showing a pattern of substantial and significant correlations across measures, including some of which are clearly distinct in content a priori (e.g., belief in pseudoscience, unwarranted conspiracy theories, and pseudo-profound bullshit).
text.formatted: The findings generally provide evidence for weak generality <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bensley et al., 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bensley et al., , 2022;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Lobato et al., 2014)</ref>, showing a pattern of substantial and significant correlations across measures, including some of which are clearly distinct in content a priori (e.g., belief in pseudoscience, unwarranted conspiracy theories, and pseudo-profound bullshit).

text.text: Although the correlations were slightly lower in Study 2, most of them remained highly significant and of substantial magnitude in the ESEM robustness analyses using target rotation in both studies.
At the same time, the findings do not clearly support strong generality-that is, a general or common factor did not adequately account for the systematic covariance across the variety of measures.
There was some weak or partial support for strong generality in Study 1, as indicated by acceptable model fit based on absolute fit indices (RMSEA and SRMR) for the bifactor model.

However, the bifactor model still fit substantially worse than the correlated factors model even in Study 1, despite the generally high fitting propensity of bifactor models noted in the literature (e.g., Greene et al., 2019).
text.formatted: However, the bifactor model still fit substantially worse than the correlated factors model even in Study 1, despite the generally high fitting propensity of bifactor models noted in the literature (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Greene et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, both SRMR and RMSEA tend to give overly optimistic fit estimates in models with many degrees of freedom and large sample sizes (Kenny et al., 2015; Shi et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Moreover, both SRMR and RMSEA tend to give overly optimistic fit estimates in models with many degrees of freedom and large sample sizes <ref type="bibr">(Kenny et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b100">Shi et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: On the other hand, CFI has a general tendency to display worse fit for models with many indicators (Kenny & McCoach, 2003).
text.formatted: On the other hand, CFI has a general tendency to display worse fit for models with many indicators <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Kenny & McCoach, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: In short, attempting to use any one-size-fits-all cut-off criteria to judge model fit is an endeavour fraught with perils and surrounded by controversy (e.g., Bazzoli, 2024; Edwards, 2013; Hancock & Mueller, 2011; Marsh et al., 2004; McNeish & Manapat, 2024; McNeish et al., 2018; Nguyen, 2025; Preacher, 2006; Shi et al., 2018).

text.text: Furthermore, while ECV indicated that roughly half of the common variance among latent factors (61% in Study 1; 47% in Study 2) was attributable to the general factor, this is still below the mean ECV of the pool of bifactor models examined in Rodriguez et al. (2016) and considerably short of the .7-.8 range that would be expected with a dominant general factor.

text.text: Furthermore, given the probable presence of many unmodeled small yet non-zero cross-loadings in the bifactor models and the far from ideal model fit of these models, the ECVs reported are likely, if anything, overestimating the strength of a general factor (Reise, 2012), as the omitted crossloadings end up being absorbed by the general factor.
