text.text: The strong generality hypothesis can therefore be considered rejected.

While Smallpage et al. (2023) provided a test of a hierarchical structure of misinformation (a second-order factor explained the covariation between conspiracy mentality, pseudoscientific, and paranormal beliefs), the model they tested contained three first-order factors, making it hard to differentiate from a correlated factors model.

Furthermore, as noted in the literature (e.g., Savalei, 2018; Xia & Yang, 2019), fit evaluation using weighted least squares based estimators can be problematic to evaluate using traditional, ML-based points of reference.
text.formatted: Furthermore, as noted in the literature (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">Savalei, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b115">Xia & Yang, 2019)</ref>, fit evaluation using weighted least squares based estimators can be problematic to evaluate using traditional, ML-based points of reference.

text.text: Using a large number of indicators and first-order factors along with MLR-estimation made it possible for us to test and evaluate the strong generality hypothesis more directly.
Do these results imply that it would be misguided to calculate a general score for misinformation susceptibility?
From a pragmatic viewpoint, interpretable aggregated scores could be provided by hierarchical measurement models, absent strict unidimensionality (Yang & Green, 2015).
text.formatted: From a pragmatic viewpoint, interpretable aggregated scores could be provided by hierarchical measurement models, absent strict unidimensionality <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Yang & Green, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, not even IQ scores are fully unidimensional, representing domainspecific cognitive skills and abilities beyond general intelligence (g), but this does not necessarily detract from the usefulness of the g-factor model (Colom et al., 2002).
text.formatted: Indeed, not even IQ scores are fully unidimensional, representing domainspecific cognitive skills and abilities beyond general intelligence (g), but this does not necessarily detract from the usefulness of the g-factor model <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Colom et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: However, misinformation susceptibility fell substantially below a priori thresholds in terms of ECV in the current studies.

Furthermore, while misinformation susceptibility may share similarities with broad trait domains (e.g., extraversion or neuroticism) in terms of its structure, it is likely more difficult to capture with a single generic hierarchical model.

This is because misinformation is a broad theoretical concept covering a vast universe of exemplars that is difficult (if not impossible) to pin down in its entirety, and there are likely multiple ways to partition it into facets depending on which specific exemplars are included in any given study.
In these respects, misinformation susceptibility may be more similar to the concept of political ideology.

Although we know today that political ideology is not reducible to a single left-right dimension, and there are a multitude of more fine-grained models of ideology (Feldman & Johnston, 2014; Nilsson et al., 2020; Schwartz et al., 2010), the left-right dimension remains widely treated as a practically useful, course-grained model of general ideology (Kteily & Brandt, 2024).
text.formatted: Although we know today that political ideology is not reducible to a single left-right dimension, and there are a multitude of more fine-grained models of ideology <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Feldman & Johnston, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">Nilsson et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">Schwartz et al., 2010)</ref>, the left-right dimension remains widely treated as a practically useful, course-grained model of general ideology <ref type="bibr">(Kteily & Brandt, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Analogously, it may be possible to assess general aspects of misinformation susceptibility, such as a general tendency to believe in unwarranted conspiracy theories, although we need to keep in mind that such models are unlikely to adequately capture the entire domain.
Conspiratorial Content.
Beyond generalities across all categories of misinformation, another source of covariation in the data was whether the misinformation represented conspiratorial content or not.
The results show a high degree of generality across different kinds of conspiratorial beliefs, albeit with some additional variation attributable to ideological tilt.

A model that divided the initial second-order factor up into two correlated second-order factors, representing conspiratorial and non-conspiratorial content, respectively, yielded a considerable improvement in model fit in Study 2.

Although the change in model fit was low in Study 1 in particular, and the two second-order factors remained very strongly correlated even in Study 2, these results should be interpreted with caution, as it is highly likely given the size of the model that latent correlations and ostensible overlap between factors were likely considerably inflated by the sheer amount of cross-loadings fixed to zero.

Taken together, the results suggest that there is a distinct dimension of susceptibility to unwarranted conspiracy theories-that is, some people are more susceptible to misinformation when it is framed in terms of a conspiratorial narrative.
This is likely one of the drivers of the lack of strong generality in the data.
The latent correlations suggest that there was more of a common core across the measures with conspiratorial content.
This is not surprising, as the non-conspiratorial measures were grouped together based on what they are not, rather than what they have in common.
Unlike the conspiratorial content, they did not align with a common worldview.

Analyses taking the ideological tilt of the misinformation into consideration even more clearly demonstrate that the congruence between the misinformation and people's worldviews was a source of covariation in the data.

A second-order model where we divided up the constructs according to their a priori ideological tilt (right-wing, neutral, and left-wing) resulted in substantially improved model fit compared to the other secondorder models for both studies, suggesting that ideological alignment was a contributing factor.
Additionally, these results are consistent with the notion that specific conspiracy theories are often contaminated by ideological content (Imhoff et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Additionally, these results are consistent with the notion that specific conspiracy theories are often contaminated by ideological content <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Imhoff et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Interestingly, there was a clearer common core across the right-wing forms of misinformation than the left-wing or neutral ones.
There are several possible explanations for this asymmetry.
First, it might arise due to differences in misinformation susceptibility between ideological groups.

Insofar as social conservatives are more epistemically vulnerable on average (e.g., Nilsson et al., 2024; Smallpage et al., 2023), their responses may to a greater extent drive correlations between the factors, resulting in higher correlations between measures with conservative content.
text.formatted: Insofar as social conservatives are more epistemically vulnerable on average (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Nilsson et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Smallpage et al., 2023)</ref>, their responses may to a greater extent drive correlations between the factors, resulting in higher correlations between measures with conservative content.

text.text: Second, the asymmetry in question may be rooted in differential exposure.

Insofar as misinformation is currently more often spread on the political right than on the left (Garrett & Bond, 2021), right-wingers should be more likely to adopt an entire "package" of misinformed beliefs from elite political discourse and ingroup authorities.
text.formatted: Insofar as misinformation is currently more often spread on the political right than on the left <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Garrett & Bond, 2021)</ref>, right-wingers should be more likely to adopt an entire "package" of misinformed beliefs from elite political discourse and ingroup authorities.

text.text: Third, it may be that the right-wing forms of misinformation, such as global warming denial and conspiracy theories about liberal elites, in themselves represent more of a coherent ideological package, whereas some forms of misinformation that we assumed would be characteristic of the left, such as IQ-denial and blank slateism, are less integrated in contemporary left-wing ideological discourse.
A different selection of scales might have resulted in higher correlations between left-leaning contents.
Science-Related Content.
Another potential source of covariation between measures is the extent to which they capture familiarity with scientific results or intellectual discourse.
In an exploratory factor analysis of unfounded beliefs, Bensley et al. (2020) found distinct (but strongly correlated) factors representing conspiracy-and science-related content.
text.formatted: In an exploratory factor analysis of unfounded beliefs, <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Bensley et al. (2020)</ref> found distinct (but strongly correlated) factors representing conspiracy-and science-related content.

text.text: In the current research, IQ-denial and blank slateism were relatively unique compared to other forms of misinformation receptivity.

Although these are commonly referred to as examples of science-related misinformation on the left (e.g., Lewandowsky & Oberauer, 2016), those exposed to it may in reality constitute a small minority (i.e., individuals in particular intellectual circles or educational milieus), compared to, for example, those exposed to misinformation about global warming.
text.formatted: Although these are commonly referred to as examples of science-related misinformation on the left (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Lewandowsky & Oberauer, 2016)</ref>, those exposed to it may in reality constitute a small minority (i.e., individuals in particular intellectual circles or educational milieus), compared to, for example, those exposed to misinformation about global warming.

text.text: Analogously, Nilsson et al. (2024) found that although individuals with progressive values were more susceptible to pseudo-profound bullshit with left-wing jargon, they were not more susceptible to postmodern bullshit, plausibly reflecting low familiarity with postmodernism among the general public.
text.formatted: Analogously, <ref type="bibr">Nilsson et al. (2024)</ref> found that although individuals with progressive values were more susceptible to pseudo-profound bullshit with left-wing jargon, they were not more susceptible to postmodern bullshit, plausibly reflecting low familiarity with postmodernism among the general public.

text.text: Alternatively, it could be that IQ-denial and blank slateism are perceived as more plausible and intuitively defensible for many who would otherwise correctly identify other forms of science-related misinformation, because environmental determinism used to be a respected account in the nature-nurture debate only decades ago (Pinker, 2006; Plomin et al., 1994).
text.formatted: Alternatively, it could be that IQ-denial and blank slateism are perceived as more plausible and intuitively defensible for many who would otherwise correctly identify other forms of science-related misinformation, because environmental determinism used to be a respected account in the nature-nurture debate only decades ago <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">(Pinker, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">Plomin et al., 1994)</ref>.

text.text: Given that the epistemic warrant for these beliefs has changed relatively recently, whether people endorse them may reflect their broader worldviews more than a domainindependent susceptibility to science-related misinformation.

Another theoretically meaningful finding was that there were particularly strong correlations between factors representing belief in conspiracy theories about a coverup of extraterrestrial activity, paranormal phenomena, and astrology.

What these have in common is a belief in unobservable, mystical entities, such as ghosts, spirits, and extraterrestrials, and mystical or magical forms of causation that are not consistent with a scientific worldview, including effects of celestial bodies on personality and the possibility of interacting with the dead.

Therefore, the results suggest that a mystical worldview constitutes an additional source of variation in misinformation susceptibility, beyond generalities, conspiratorial content, ideology, and science knowledge.

Although belief in pseudoscience correlated strongly with these types of misinformation susceptibility, it also correlated strongly with measures capturing, for example, other types of conspiratorial thinking.

This is likely because this measure covered a multitude of pseudoscientific ideas, some of which are more aligned with mysticism, such as the law of attraction, and some of which are more aligned with general or science-related conspiratorial narratives without entailing a mystical worldview, such as anti-vaccination discourse.
One potential cause for concern is the misfit of the second-order models, according to the incremental fit indices.

Given the size of these models and the mediocre model fit, there is cause for concern that model misspecification may be inflating parameter estimates (Asparouhov & Muthén, 2009; Maydeu-Olivares, 2017).
text.formatted: Given the size of these models and the mediocre model fit, there is cause for concern that model misspecification may be inflating parameter estimates <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Asparouhov & Muthén, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Maydeu-Olivares, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, the standard errors associated with the factor loadings were generally larger than what might be expected given our sample size.
This may suggest some added degree of instability (uncertainty) in our estimates.
However, this concern may be alleviated to some extent by the large sample size of both of our studies, meaning that the absolute sizes of the standard errors are still relatively small.
Another limitation is that we did not investigate the underlying psychological factors that drive the structure of misinformation susceptibility.

Some factors, such as higher intuitive and subjectivist thinking, and lower analytical and actively open-minded thinking, plausibly yield higher general misinformation susceptibility across domains (e.g., Aspernäs et al., 2023; Bensley et al., 2022; Pennycook et al., 2015; Ståhl & van Prooijen, 2018; Torres et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Some factors, such as higher intuitive and subjectivist thinking, and lower analytical and actively open-minded thinking, plausibly yield higher general misinformation susceptibility across domains (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Aspernäs et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Bensley et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">Pennycook et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b103">Ståhl & van Prooijen, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b106">Torres et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Others may have more local effects.

For example, distrust in experts may yield higher susceptibility specifically to misinformation with a conspiratorial or science-related component, at least in cultures that value science (Bensley et al., 2022), but it should be less relevant to bullshit receptivity.
text.formatted: For example, distrust in experts may yield higher susceptibility specifically to misinformation with a conspiratorial or science-related component, at least in cultures that value science <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bensley et al., 2022)</ref>, but it should be less relevant to bullshit receptivity.

text.text: Similarly, political partisanship or extremism, scientific knowledge, and religiosity may matter particularly for misinformation with ideologically congruent, science-related, or mystical components, respectively (e.g., Lindeman & Aarnio, 2006; Washburn & Skitka, 2018).
text.formatted: Similarly, political partisanship or extremism, scientific knowledge, and religiosity may matter particularly for misinformation with ideologically congruent, science-related, or mystical components, respectively (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Lindeman & Aarnio, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Washburn & Skitka, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, hypersensitive detection of agency and purpose in the material world may particularly predict susceptibility to conspiracy theories, paranormal beliefs, and some forms of pseudoscience (e.g., Boudry et al., 2015; Douglas et al., 2016), rather than other forms of science misinformation or bullshit; and threat sensitivity may predict receptivity to misinformation with conspiratorial or in other ways threat-evoking content (Van Prooijen & Vugt, 2018).
text.formatted: Furthermore, hypersensitive detection of agency and purpose in the material world may particularly predict susceptibility to conspiracy theories, paranormal beliefs, and some forms of pseudoscience (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Boudry et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Douglas et al., 2016)</ref>, rather than other forms of science misinformation or bullshit; and threat sensitivity may predict receptivity to misinformation with conspiratorial or in other ways threat-evoking content <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">(Van Prooijen & Vugt, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Further research is needed to rigorously test which explanations hold up across which forms of misinformation.

Future studies that investigate multiple potential sources of systematic covariation beyond a general misinformation susceptibility (e.g., conspiracy theories, mysticism, essentialism, trust in science, knowledge about science, political ideology), should consider including marker variables or other approaches to assess presence of systematic method covariance in the data.
Although we collected data from two countries with a large and diverse battery of measures, the extent to which the conclusions generalize to other measures and countries is unknown.
A potential complication is that misinformation susceptibility may be contingent upon the information environment people are immersed in, which varies across cultures and shifts over time.

While we anticipate that the general categories recur universally (e.g., conspiratorial, ideological, science-related, and mystical content), the specific exemplars that are most relevant within a given context may vary.
Therefore, it may be difficult to create a single standardized measurement that holds across time and place.
Further research is thus needed to develop measurements calibrated to various settings, while assessing the stability of the general conceptual structure.

To this end, we recommend that researchers focus on general types of misinformation (e.g., pseudoscience, unwarranted conspiracy theories, and pseudoprofound bullshit) rather than specific "fake news" stories, which go out of date quickly and generalize poorly across populations.

Furthermore, it may be worthwhile to investigate whether the structure of misinformation susceptibility is more constrained by elite discourse and propaganda in autocratic regimes than in democracies (Dunwoody et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Furthermore, it may be worthwhile to investigate whether the structure of misinformation susceptibility is more constrained by elite discourse and propaganda in autocratic regimes than in democracies <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Dunwoody et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, future studies should investigate whether conspiracy theories are less integrated into the misinformation network in societies with higher levels or political and institutional corruption, where at least some of them may have higher epistemic warrant (Alper & Imhoff, 2022).
text.formatted: Additionally, future studies should investigate whether conspiracy theories are less integrated into the misinformation network in societies with higher levels or political and institutional corruption, where at least some of them may have higher epistemic warrant <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Alper & Imhoff, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This would shed further light on the degree to which the associations are driven by the implausibility of the contents rather than the conspiratorial narratives per se (Frenken et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This would shed further light on the degree to which the associations are driven by the implausibility of the contents rather than the conspiratorial narratives per se <ref type="bibr">(Frenken et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The findings across two studies suggest that there is a clear degree of generality across different aspects of misinformation susceptibility, as evidenced by generally substantial and significant latent correlations across measures (i.e., generality in the weaker sense).

This generality is not strong enough to be adequately captured by a general factor (i.e., generality in the stronger sense), however, suggesting that the type and content of the misinformationfor example, whether it incorporates a conspiratorial or ideological narrative or elements of mysticism, magical thinking, or science denial-still plays a considerable role.
These findings suggest that it is advantageous to divide misinformation susceptibility into several interrelated domains rather than treating it as a single homogeneous dimension.
